stories.topic: The Life Lessons Meetup in Goa
stories.summary: After three cohorts of their online course Life Lessons in 2025, Amit and Ajay organised an in-person meetup in Goa. They expected 20-30 attendees; over 50 came, paying their own flights and hotels, including last-minute additions from Thailand and New York. Ajay describes it as 'better than anything I anticipated'; Amit, a self-described socially awkward introvert, found it the only large gathering of his life where he felt fully comfortable, partly because the steep price point had created a selection effect for people of agency, curiosity, and 'hutke' thinking.
stories.insight: A premium price point and high effort can be a feature, not a bug — they filter for the kind of community you actually want. The communities of choice the internet enables can be more meaningful than the communities of circumstance we are born into.

stories.topic: The CEO and the Three Lovers (Narendra Shenoy's Joke)
stories.summary: A CEO ready to settle down gives each of his three girlfriends a million dollars to test them. The first uses it to beautify herself for him; the second buys him gadgets (including a Sony FX3 and XM4 headphones); the third invests it in diversified ETFs across mature democracies and turns it into three million. Whom does he choose? The one with the biggest boobs.
stories.insight: A wickedly compact illustration of the chapter's headline finding: men's revealed visual preference often overrides every other rational consideration. The setup primes you to expect rationality; the punchline insists on hardware.

stories.summary: Around 2006-2007, the Indian erotic comic strip Savita Bhabhi was going viral. Amit, then writing his prolific blog India Uncut (eight thousand posts in five years), wrote about it. One day he opened a new edition of the strip to discover that Savita Bhabhi was talking about her favourite blog — and it was India Uncut.
stories.insight: A self-deprecating moment of pride that doubles as cultural archaeology — pre-Twitter virality flowing through bloggers and naughty comic strips. Amit calls it one of the highlights of his life.

stories.topic: Kinsey Was Right So Trivially That His Treatment Boggles The Mind
stories.summary: Alfred Kinsey asked 521 questions of thousands of respondents and produced his books on male (1948) and female (1953) sexuality, busting myths — that homosexuality was rare deviance, that women didn't experience sexual desire. The Rockefeller Foundation dropped his funding, he was ostracised, and he died of pneumonia at 62. Amit pairs him with Ignaz Semmelweis, who pioneered surgical hand-washing and died in a lunatic asylum.
stories.insight: The pattern: pioneers who tell society uncomfortable truths often die punished, only to be vindicated trivially decades later. The lesson cuts both ways — for would-be truth-tellers, and for the rest of us in how we treat them in their lifetime.

stories.summary: In a study, women were asked to smell the body odour of around fifty men in a blind test. The men they rated as sexiest by smell turned out to be the men who were most dominant and high-status. Neither the women nor the men knew what was actually being detected.
stories.insight: Mate-evaluation operates at levels far below conscious awareness. We think we know why we are attracted to someone; the actual machinery is running in modules we cannot introspect.

stories.topic: Ovulation, Lap Dancers, and Subliminal Male Protectiveness
stories.summary: A study tracked tips received by lap dancers across menstrual cycle phases — ovulating women earned the highest tips by far, then non-menstruating, then menstruating. Either the women were behaving more sexily, or men were subconsciously detecting fertility, or both. Even more striking: men become more protective of their female partners during ovulation, despite having no conscious way to know when their partner is ovulating.
stories.insight: A vivid demonstration of communication channels we have no introspective access to. The body is broadcasting and receiving signals our conscious minds cannot read — and behaviour is reshaping itself accordingly.

stories.topic: Miss Marple's Detective Agency at the CIA
stories.summary: Responding to Amit's frame of women carrying four 'detectives' in their heads (social, cultural, emotional, physical), Ajay reflects that our pop-culture image of intelligence work is masculine — Le Carre, Bond — but the actual traits required (vast pattern-holding, noticing one thing falling out of pattern) match the female cognitive profile. He notes that critical analysts in the CIA's hunt for Osama bin Laden were women, and proposes — half-seriously — that India's intelligence rebuild should hire many more women.
stories.insight: Sexual selection pressures may have shaped a specific cognitive style — broad relational pattern-detection — that translates into real-world institutional advantage. Aligning hiring with what actually drives the work, rather than with gendered iconography, is a free lunch.

recommendations.creator: Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam
recommendations.context: The central book of the episode — a 2011 study using over a billion data points from internet search and behavior to map revealed sexual preferences, then explaining them through evolutionary biology, psychology, and sociology.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it the single most comprehensive picture of what we actually want sexually — a leap forward from Kinsey's stated preferences to revealed preferences at internet scale. Most pages are underlined; many phenomena Amit had taken for granted were finally explained in 'high definition.'

recommendations.item: Sexual Behavior in the Human Male
recommendations.creator: Alfred Kinsey and others
recommendations.context: Kinsey's 1948 landmark report based on 521-question surveys of thousands of American men.
recommendations.reason: Foundational for the modern empirical study of human sexuality — busted the myth that homosexual experience was a fringe deviance and forced society to confront the gap between professed and actual behaviour.

recommendations.item: Sexual Behavior in the Human Female
recommendations.creator: Alfred Kinsey and others
recommendations.context: Kinsey's 1953 companion volume on female sexuality.
recommendations.reason: The book that shattered the Victorian-era assumption that women did not experience sexual desire or pleasure — and got Kinsey defunded by the Rockefeller Foundation for the trouble.

recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Dawkins's 1975 popular-science classic that re-frames evolution from the gene's-eye view.
recommendations.reason: Amit's first major milestone in popular science writing on natural selection. Required background for everything else in the field — though Amit cautions readers to take 'selfish' as metaphor, not literal psychology.

recommendations.creator: Donald Symons
recommendations.context: Symons's 1979 book using natural selection tools to explain why men and women are wired differently in their sexual desires.
recommendations.reason: Amit's second great milestone in popular evolutionary writing after Dawkins. The book that opened up the field of using natural-selection logic to explain human sexual behaviour, and the source of much that A Billion Wicked Thoughts builds on.

recommendations.creator: Steven Pinker
recommendations.context: Pinker's case against the dogma that the human mind has no innate structure.
recommendations.reason: How Amit personally entered the field of natural selection in the early 2000s. Source of the line 'nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them' — and of the provocative argument that art and culture themselves may be male ornamentation.

recommendations.creator: Geoffrey Miller
recommendations.context: Miller's argument that human cognitive abilities — including art, language, and creativity — evolved primarily through sexual selection.
recommendations.reason: Part of the canonical reading list Amit recommends for anyone serious about evolutionary explanations of human behaviour. Backbone for the claim that men are smart largely because women are selective.

recommendations.creator: David Buss
recommendations.context: Buss's data-driven survey of mate-preference differences across cultures.
recommendations.reason: One of the foundational books that opened Amit's eyes to how biology operates on human mating choices. Continues the Symons project with cross-cultural empirical evidence.

recommendations.creator: Robert Wright
recommendations.context: Wright's exploration of evolutionary psychology and how Darwinian logic plays out in everyday human relationships.
recommendations.reason: Specifically cited for its analysis of how the same underlying drives can produce both monogamy and polygamy as stable equilibria in different societies — a useful corrective to thinking any one mating system is 'natural.'

recommendations.creator: Catherine Salmon and Donald Symons
recommendations.context: Salmon and Symons's analysis of romance novels as a window into female sexual psychology.
recommendations.reason: Source of the central juxtaposition in this episode: the 'pornotopia' of male fantasy versus the 'romantotopia' of female fantasy — and the argument that the romance novel is, structurally, a chronicle of female mate choice.

recommendations.creator: Neil Strauss
recommendations.context: Strauss's 25-year-old handbook for pickup artists, using natural-selection insights to game male-female interaction.
recommendations.reason: Cited as 'perhaps the earliest handbook for incels,' but useful for the data-driven grain of truth at its core: in a competitive market, an inconsiderate-asshole signal often outperforms a polite-beta signal — explaining why women are sometimes drawn to dominant cads.

recommendations.creator: Wikipedia
recommendations.context: The Wikipedia entry for David Hume's distinction.
recommendations.reason: Linked as the philosophical guardrail for the entire episode: you cannot derive what ought to be from what is. Men being 'wired' for promiscuity does not make promiscuity right.

recommendations.creator: Wikipedia
recommendations.context: The Wikipedia entry for G.E. Moore's 1903 fallacy.
recommendations.reason: The converse of the is-ought trap — defining 'natural' as 'good' and using it to denigrate, e.g., homosexuality. Essential reading before drawing any moral conclusions from evolutionary findings.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Cross-listed in the show's standard resources as background for the broader project these podcast hosts are engaged in.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.reason: The session that became this episode was first delivered at a Life Lessons in-person meetup; the course has a detailed natural-selection webinar by Ajay that frames much of the discussion.

core_ideas.concept: Why Understanding Human Sexuality Matters: The Four Reasons
core_ideas.explanation: Amit gives four reasons this is not nudge-nudge-wink-wink material but central to self-knowledge. (1) Know thyself: without understanding our hardwiring, we gaslight ourselves about our own desires. (2) Know others: without it, we project our own value system onto people who are wired differently. (3) Increase agency: understanding the wiring is the precondition for choosing not to follow it. (4) Solve the modern-world mismatch: our instincts were tuned for hunter-gatherer scarcity, and dating apps and birth control hijack circuits meant for entirely different conditions.
core_ideas.quote: Pawn dating apps and birth control hijack ancient circuits meant for scarcity and reproduction.

core_ideas.concept: The Four Caveats Against Misreading Evolutionary Findings
core_ideas.explanation: Before any evolutionary claim about sex differences, four guardrails: (1) The is-ought fallacy — don't derive moral oughts from natural facts. (2) The naturalistic fallacy — don't define what is good as what is natural. (3) Don't confuse proximate and ultimate causation — when an evolutionary biologist says we like sweet things 'because' calories were scarce, he means at the gene-selection timescale, not in your conscious mind today. (4) All generalisations have exceptions — explanatory power at the population level does not predict any individual.
core_ideas.quote: It is a description, not a prescription. It's not justification, it's just explanation.

core_ideas.explanation: All male-female mating differences ultimately derive from one asymmetry: in ancestral conditions, a man could spread his genes at near-zero biological cost, while a woman incurred nine months of pregnancy plus years of childrearing per reproductive event. This produces two very different optimisation problems — men optimised for opportunity (be promiscuous, be widely available), women optimised for selection (filter ruthlessly because the cost of error is catastrophic). Everything downstream — visual versus narrative arousal, jealousy patterns, attraction to youth versus to status — flows from this single asymmetry.
core_ideas.quote: A man's incentives are really to spread his genes as widely as possible, as often as possible. But for women there is a cost.

core_ideas.concept: Two Selection Targets For Women: Genes vs. Provider
core_ideas.explanation: Female selectiveness optimises for two things at once that often live in different men. (1) The 'cad' or dominant male — high status, charisma, willingness to spread genes — is the partner who maximises offspring's gene-spreading prospects. (2) The 'good man' — stable, nurturing, committed — is the partner who maximises offspring's chance of reaching viability. Romance novels are the great delusion that both can be found in one body; in the real world, very few men combine both, and pretending otherwise is one source of relationship pain.
core_ideas.quote: There are like two great self-delusions, one each for men and women. The great female delusion is that they can get both men in one body.

core_ideas.explanation: The headline finding of A Billion Wicked Thoughts and the spine of the episode: men's arousal is dominated by visual cues, women's by narrative. Two percent of porn purchases are by women; ninety percent of romance-novel consumption is by women. A sixty-second visual clip can move a man to climax; the female equivalent is a 250-page book that takes hours to read. The difference is not in the strength of the drive but in the path to it — visual instants for men, embedded social-emotional context for women.
core_ideas.quote: A sixty-second clip can compel a man to masturbate to ejaculation. But the single most popular artifact used by women to generate arousal takes the form of a 250-page book that requires hours to digest.

core_ideas.explanation: Sexual selection rewards visible signals of underlying genetic quality. In ancestral conditions, the ideal female face is symmetrical across cultures because symmetry is a signal of developmental health; clear skin signals immunological health. The 0.7 waist-to-hip ratio that men consistently rate as most attractive is not a learned preference but a marker of estrogen and reproductive readiness. Even small feet correlate with high estrogen, which produces the gynoid fat distribution that yields larger breasts and butts — the cluster is a single underlying signal.
core_ideas.quote: We find symmetry beautiful because it is a sign of good health. We find clear skin beautiful because it is a sign of good health.

core_ideas.explanation: Ogas and Gaddam's frame for the female brain in mate-evaluation mode: every woman carries four detectives — a social, a cultural, an emotional, and a physical detective — running in parallel. Men have only the physical detective. This is why women remember more, are more verbal, call and text more, use conversation for connection rather than information, and are more vulnerable to anxiety, depression, and eating disorders — the agency is always working, scoring inputs, looking for misalignments.

core_ideas.concept: Psychological vs. Physical Arousal in Women
core_ideas.explanation: In men, physical and psychological arousal are essentially the same circuit. In women they are dissociated — separate brain regions, often desynchronised in time. A study showed women physically aroused by a wide spectrum of imagery (including across-species cues) but psychologically aroused by very few. The implication for the cultural debate around consent is sharp: a body's physiological response (lubrication, even orgasm) during rape is not evidence of psychological consent — these channels operate independently.

core_ideas.concept: The Power of Or vs. The Power of And
core_ideas.explanation: Ogas and Gaddam's compact frame for male versus female sexual decision-making. Male arousal runs on OR — any one sufficient cue (visible curves OR willingness OR novelty) can flip the switch. Female arousal runs on AND — physical attraction AND status AND conversation AND emotional safety AND social fit must coincide. This is why turning a man on is comparatively trivial and turning a woman on is a multi-variable optimisation problem.
core_ideas.quote: Men just are not selective, they want to do it as often as possible. It comes down to the power of or.

core_ideas.concept: Ovulation Drives Behaviour Both Sides Of The Couple
core_ideas.explanation: When women are ovulating — whether or not they consciously know it — they tend to dress more revealingly, behave more sexily, and become more open to encounters with dominant 'bad boy' types, exactly the regime where their genes most benefit from the highest-quality male. Strikingly, their male partners also become more protective during ovulation, despite having no conscious cue. The signal is being broadcast and received below the level of awareness, and behaviour on both sides reorganises around it.

core_ideas.concept: Romance, Jealousy, and Mating Systems As Adaptations
core_ideas.explanation: Romance is not 'extra' sentiment layered on top of biology — it is the adaptive glue that keeps a male around long enough to bring his offspring to viability. Jealousy is similarly functional, and male and female jealousy are different. Male jealousy is sexual: he must avoid investing resources in a child not his own. Female jealousy is emotional: she must avoid losing the provider. The same underlying drives can also produce different mating systems — both monogamy and polygamy are stable equilibria depending on the local social environment.

core_ideas.concept: Men Are Smart Because Women Are Selective
core_ideas.explanation: Pinker's argument in The Blank Slate: human cognitive achievements — art, language, conversation, eventually science — may be male ornamentation, the human version of the peacock's tail. Selection happened because females had to discriminate among males, so males had to advertise quality with elaborate, costly displays. Roughly: across history something like 80% of women but only ~30% of men have left descendants — a lopsided competition that drives men to extreme, often dangerous displays of capability.
core_ideas.quote: If you think I'm smart, it's because of you. It's my peacock's tail.

core_ideas.explanation: A wiring-level asymmetry in life goals: women are wired to be lovable (because being lovable secures a long-term provider), men are wired for greatness (because in a winner-take-most reproductive lottery, only extreme distinction earns reproductive success). Being lovable is comparatively achievable and intentional; aspiring for greatness is brutally hard and a relatively small share succeed. The pursuit of greatness is a major source of male misery, and men should consciously borrow from the female playbook — also aspire to be lovable.

A finding from A Billion Wicked Thoughts: gay men's sexual cognition matches straight men's, not straight women's — visual-dominated, focused on the same body zones, low investment in narrative. The arousal targets shift (manly chests, manly butts) but the architecture is the same. This is why gay men prefer 'straight porn' over gay porn — they want a macho man, and they find a real straight man more arousing than a man performing straight sex. The accidental side effect: 'straight porn for gay men' (with the camera on the man) attracted female viewers too, finally giving women the visual focus they had been missing.

core_ideas.concept: Madame de Stael's Asymmetry of Desire
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's closing frame for the entire episode: 'The desire of the man is for the woman; the desire of the woman is for the desire of the man.' The first-order asymmetry that the entire chapter has been mapping in detail — men's wanting is direct, women's wanting is mediated through being wanted. So much of modern relational behaviour and modern social pathology becomes legible once this asymmetry is named.
core_ideas.quote: The desire of the man is for the woman. The desire of the woman is for the desire of the man.

core_ideas.concept: Hardwiring Is Not Destiny — The Civilising Project
core_ideas.explanation: The closing ethical move of the episode and arguably its centre: knowing how we are wired is the precondition for choosing not to act on the wiring. We are hardwired for lust, for violence, for jealousy, for tribalism — every one of those instincts has cases where acting on it is monstrous. The project of civilisation is precisely to mitigate the worst of our instincts and to choose who we want to be. Denial of the hardware makes this impossible; acknowledgement is the start of agency.
core_ideas.quote: Sometimes nurture amplifies nature, sometimes it mitigates nature, which is to my mind the project of civilisation.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the Life Lessons WhatsApp average: 'On Life Lessons everybody reads an average of one paper a day. But what's really happening is 139 of us don't read papers at all, and Ajay reads 140 papers every night.'

Ajay's CIA recruitment proposal, half-joking, half-serious: rebuild Indian intelligence by hiring many more women, because Miss Marple's detective agency is exactly the cognitive style the work requires.
Amit on male wiring: 'I'm gonna mansplain to you about ovulation' — flagged immediately as a terrible thing to do, then he does it anyway.
Amit on Indian-traffic identity: 'In traffic I become a Punjabi, otherwise I'm fully Bengali.'
Amit's bawdy parody: a riff on the Beatles cover of 'My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean,' titled 'My Bodhi Lies Over the Lotion.'

Amit on hentai's design logic: everything is exaggerated — breasts massive, butts massive, male organs the size of an arm — because the medium has figured out it is all about visual cues, and people don't actually need to be in the picture.
Amit on aging mid-sentence: 'Who we them. Who we them. Gentle readers, I'm sorry, we are growing old. Enjoy these episodes while they last.'
Amit on adulthood: 'Nobody grows up. There are no adults. Adulting is the biggest con job they tell you.'
Ajay's closing pretty line: 'Men love women, women love children, children love kittens — there is no reciprocation.'
Amit's tongue-in-cheek warning to readers about clipping: he is 'terrified that people will take clips from later in the episode and just put them up by themselves, devoid of context.'
Amit on the Savita Bhabhi blog cameo: opening a new edition of the comic to find Savita Bhabhi citing India Uncut as her favourite blog — 'what greater achievement could there be?'
'Know thyself' — the inscription at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, paired with Socrates's 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' framing the entire epistemic motivation for the episode.

'Internet Rule 34' — if you can think of it, there is porn of it. Used to mark the long tail of preferences alongside the heavy concentration of just twenty search terms accounting for eighty percent of porn searches.
Donald Symons: 'To encounter erotica designed to appeal to the other sex is to gaze into the psychological abyss that separates the sexes.'
Steven Pinker: 'Nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them' — the standing one-line answer to nature-vs-nurture as a false binary.

Ignaz Semmelweis — the surgeon who pioneered hand-washing, was ostracised, and died in a lunatic asylum. Invoked as a parallel to Kinsey: pioneers society punishes in their lifetime and vindicates only in retrospect.

Charles Sobhraj — the serial killer who continued to attract female admirers from prison, used as evidence that women's hardwired attraction to extreme dominance does not switch off in the presence of monstrous behaviour.
Neil Strauss in The Game: 'You don't have to be an asshole. But if you have no choice, being an inconsiderate asshole beats being a polite beta every time.'

The Flame and the Flower — the first romance novel published straight to paperback (1972), which defined the genre and opens with the hero raping the heroine before she 'tames' him — a paradigm case of the wild-coconut fantasy.

The Amazon search statistic: 415 millionaires, 286 billionaires, and 263 sheikhs in romance-novel titles — including 'The Millionaire Secretary,' 'The Billionaire's Virgin Bride,' and 'The Sheikh's Secret Harem Girl.'
The 'taming the wild coconut' trope — hard on the outside, soft on the inside — as the dominant fantasy structure of the romance novel: meet a cad, tame the cad, the cad becomes the husband.
Madame de Stael: 'The desire of the man is for the woman. The desire of the woman is for the desire of the man.'
Ogas and Gaddam's opening line: 'Scientists have an easier time gazing at intergalactic quasars than peeking into someone's bedroom.'
